## 4. The Right Stuff (1983) was originally a box office flop despite being one of the best films about the early space race between the Soviet Union and the United States

**Score:** 441
**Body:** I just rewatched The Right Stuff with my son and the film is as great as it was when I first saw it in the 80’s.

In 1983 the Right Stuff was released with an amazing ensemble cast which included Ed Harris, Scott Glen, Dennis Quaid, Jeff Goldblum, and the now legendary portrayal of Chuck Yeager by Sam Sheppard. The movie is a wonderful salute to America and her space program and the movie is expertly written, cast, and executed from it’s blending of actual archival footage into scenes to it incredible use of insect noises whenever the press corps or journalists are on the screen.

The movie won 4 oscars out of its 8 nominations, so you can imagine how shocked I was today when I learned that the movie was a financial failure at the box office. It made only 21 million against a 27 million dollar budget.

It seems that a large swath of people initially avoided going to see the movie in theaters for a specific reason. Astronaut turned U.S. senator John Glenn portrayed wonderfully in the movie by Ed Harris was running for President of the United States at the time. People feared the movie was essentially a multimillion dollar campaign ad instead of one of the best crafted films of the 20th century.

I would recommend this movie to anyone who hasn’t seen it. It beautifully tells the story of the early days of NASA and the original Mercury Seven Astronauts despite being a box office dud on first arrival.

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. No bucks. No Buck Rogers.
  - Who’s the best pilot you ever saw?
    - My father (who was a military aviator) said that to my mom all the time.
2. Very good film and had a great cast: Ed Harris, Dennis Quaid, Scott Glenn, Fred Ward, Barbara Hershey, Sam Shepard
  - I still find it hilarious that Jeff Goldblum and Harry Shearer were the two NASA recruiters.
  - During the rewatch, everyone hits their scenes out of the park. Dozens of actors I probably can’t even name with just a couple of lines here and there are absolutely amazing. Quality start to finish.
3. The book, especially the description of the final Yeager flight, is amazing as it is graphic. Chuck was one tough sob.


Is that a man? Yer goddammit right it is!
4. Probably my favorite space-themed movie, and one of the most talented ensemble casts of all time. Gus Grissom was probably my favorite Fred Ward role, and Dennis Quaid was at his peak.
5. My mom was a model rocket enthusiast when I was growing up, we had this on half the time we were building rockets.  One of the few films from my childhood that got better with age, the emphasis on the astronauts as human being rather than heroes matters a lot more when you're over 30.

I like how the film portrays Chuck Yaeger as the quintessential stick-and-rudder man, perhaps a little too great at being a pilot to make for a good astronaut.  Also, John Glenn is so goddamn perfect it would be irritating if the guy wasn't also so damn likeable.

And the hatch just blew, NASA later confirmed it.
6. “Is it dangerous?”

(In my top 10 greatest movies. Should’ve won best picture but glad Conti won best score which is beautiful. Waiting for the 4K release)

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. What do people mean when they say all films should be/are political?

**Score:** 0
**Body:** What is politics in cinema exactly? If politics in cinema is simply depicting a world or people shaped by that world, yes every film is inherently political. But every film shouldn’t have a political message, right? Sometimes the message should be about humans. Like Truffaut thought. If I’m not wrong he thought that an artist can be politically active as a citizen, but art itself should not be forced to serve an ideological agenda and it should be free to explore beauty, love, childhood, and personal human longing. Some people just see Godard saying *"We're talking about solidarity with students and workers, and you're talking about tracking shots and close-ups!"* during May '68 and think they’re the most socialist people ever and for them every film that doesn’t have a strict political message is bad. I’ve seen lots of people like that. Like what makes people think that? For example last winter during Berlinale Wenders said:

"Movies can change the world but not in a political way. No movie has really changed any politician’s idea, but … we can change the idea that people have of how they should live. We have to stay out of politics because if we make movies that are dedicatedly political, we enter the field of politics. But we are the counterweight of politics, we are the opposite of politics. We have to do the work of people, not the work of politicians." 

And people got incredibly mad at him but I still haven’t understood exactly what drove people mad in his sentences. Films with overly didactic political messages mostly just end up being bad, and cinema is the most human art there is isnt it? Why do people force it to be overly politic, isn’t that killing the human side of cinema? Or people don’t mean it that way and I’m understanding it wrong. But I don’t think what Wenders said is wrong. Apocalypse Now made a whole generation of Americans realize how outright unjust their involvement in Vietnam was yet it still didnt change a politicians view. The Gulf War still happened. Russo-Ukranian war happened after Come and See. Isnt he right when he says no film has ever changed a politicians ideas?

I’m at a conflict when it comes to this subject. I’m not trying to make a point here. I just want to know what makes people think that way of art and politics. I’d just want to discuss please. I just need some light shined upon this subject please.

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. "we can change the idea that people have of how they should live"

This is what politics is all about.  Politics is not the business of politicians.  It is the business of The People.  Politicians are just hired hands doing a job we specify.  At least, ideally. 

The point about it being didactic and forced is a fair one.  But there's nothing more human than politics. 
2. > Sometimes the message should be about humans.

Politics have a direct impact on many humans and the reality they live in. And often times, those disenfranchised have their life politicized wether they like it or not. 

You mention exploring love for example. Imagine a movie of a trans person in rom com that doesn't acknowledge that she's trans outside of her just being trans. To people of a certain view, the idea that a trans woman is exactly like a woman assigned at birth is not only wrong politically, but morally offensive. 

And I think that gets to the idea of why "Everything is political." Is so popular now. Many people, thanks to social media, see the direct impact of our politics on peoples every day life. It's no longer this thing you do at an arena, and once you leave or call uncle ends and everyone can go back to forgetting about it. We no longer believe that our desirex end goal is the same, that the status quo or basic decency we should expect for all people is the same. 

So even a movie with a simple message like "You should care care for everyone and protect each other" is going to be questioned when we see people in our daily lives, social media, or politics that we see as downright evil or malicious. 

Re: your statement about didactic or heavily political films being bad. 

I heavily disagree with this. The Green Mile has a clear stance that the death penalty is a wrong and cruel event for everyone involved. Portrait of a Woman On Fire is seen as one of the greatest films of all time and is a fiercely feminist film. Jennie Delman, Battle of Algiers, Y Tu Mama Tambien, I Am Cuba, etc etc. I could list films forever.
  - I think our definition of didactic differs. I definitely wouldn’t consider Jeanne Dielman didactically political. If she joined a woman’s rights movement it would be didactically political. But she doesn’t. The film is feminist because it shows how painfully mundane her life is. It’s quite the opposite of didactic. It has a political message but it is miles away from being didactic. It’s slow-burn and introspective, not in any way didactic. Every film that has a clear political message is not didactic in my opinion. Films like The Green Mile isn’t didactic in my opinion too. They are subtle when it comes to their political messages. 
    - Didactic doesn't mean unsubtle though. It means something made with the purpose of imposing a moral or lesson. Some people see it as overly perspective but I think that's not useful because that's subjective. 

Dielman is also incredibly unsubtle in the painfully mundane and empty life it's showing for homemakers and mothers. It's not subtle in what it's boring you into learning at all. 
3. There's a cold war joke that exemplifies it perfectly:

> In a conversation between a CIA agent and a KGB operative: "I have to admit, I'm always so impressed by Soviet propaganda. You really know how to get people worked up," the CIA agent says.

>"Thank you," the KGB says. "We do our best but truly, it's nothing compared to American propaganda. Your people believe everything your state media tells them."

>The CIA agent drops his drink in shock and disgust. "Thank you friend, but you must be confused... There's no propaganda in America."


Every film is political because every film carries an ideology, regardless of whether it's intentional or not. Marvel movies are filled with ideology, spousing intervention and exceptionalism, their entire foundation as a genre is based on that, even if they sell themselves as apolitical. What people who call out that all art is inherently political warn is that the hidden politics are the most dangerous ones, because they don't want you to think about them, just internalize their messages — to the point that even the people making those films are not realizing the politics of their own works.
  - I think Wenders also said once "Every film is political. Most political of all are those that pretend not to be: 'entertainment' movies. They are the most political films there are  
because they dismiss the possibility of change. In every frame they tell you everything's fine the way it is. They are a continual advertisement for things as they are" and that goes with what you said.
4. A film doesn't have to be didactic or overtly ideological to be political. 

You mention beauty, love, childhood, personal human longing. I think we have a recent good example just from the first. Who or what constitutes what's "beautiful?" 

Some people were angry that Lupita Nyong'o was cast as Helen of Troy. The people who reacted negatively to her casting derided it as "political," claimed she wasn't beautiful enough, or wasn't beautiful in the right way. But the movie itself doesn't make a point of her race at all—not in dialogue, not in framing. She's just… playing that part while happening to be black. (And I think many would say you can fairly describe her as uncommonly beautiful.) But because race and beauty standards are so linked, it was interpreted as a "political" choice. 

Love: what kinds of love are normal? Appropriate? Not appropriate? 

Childhood: what's a normal childhood? What's an unconventional childhood? What's appropriate for children? What isn't?

Longing: are there any societal barriers to what the character is longing for?

Even the vast majority of movies that aren't trying to be ideological usually imply answers to these questions. They probably even don't make a point of answering, but we, as the meme goes, "live in a society." It's nearly impossible to tell any kind of story without touching upon issues that might touch societal (AKA political) topics. That's what is meant by "everything is political." 
5. I think many people mistake politics to include a very narrow set of issues and considerations, both in and outside film. Politics is not limited to what someone’s opinion on war, abortion or a specific politician is, it involves the organization of civil society and how people live together. Political and social concerns are highly intertwined.

I don’t think every film has to be overly didactic to be considered to be political. For example The Irishman is a highly political film, it tells the story of a man who throughout his life that participated in the corruption of civic and social institutions, such as the Teamsters and the Presidency. Its examination of the mid to late 20th century presents the line between organized crime and “legitimate” government as porous and interactive. 

I think it would be better to say that there are political elements to most films that people may not realize. The topics and considerations of “political elements” may be debated but films that focus on war, racial prejudice (Blackkklansman), the nature of women and what they are capable of (Little Women), religious rights (Silence), law enforcement (all Noir and trial films), in my opinion all have political characteristics to them and should be treated as such
6. Politics informs just about everything, and inversely just about everything is political. Politics exists in the infrastructure that we build our lives around, the societies we live in, the way we see ourselves and those around us. 

You think a film being about humans and their emotions isn’t political? There are so many deeply felt human stories that are considered political just by virtue of who they focus on. Look at a movie like *Moonlight.* It’s mostly about love, longing and a man coming to terms with who he is. But just by nature of the setting, it’s informed by poverty, the American school system and historical segregation. It’s also about gay Black men, and choosing to make stories focused on minority populations is unfortunately considered a political act by many. 

Movies that take place in the real world are set somewhere that’s shaped by politics. Movies taking place in worlds of fantasy take place in settings that are informed by the author’s experiences and beliefs, which themselves are informed by politics. 

Even movies that are purely cynical product are political in their way. *The Emoji Movie* is political by nature, simply because its existence is based around a product (smartphones). It is a monument to late capitalism. It is a reflection of the priorities of a consumerist society, and is therefore inherently political.

Maybe I’m stretching the definition of politics past what you’re intending, but these are all political issues. I’m of the mindset that there are no apolitical stories, because politics bleeds into everything in life. Politics is just the way we organize ourselves as a species. 

## 2. Talking about the negatives and positives of the Odyssea

**Score:** 0
**Body:** Okay, so in my last post I just rambled on about the film because I just saw it and I thought to get things out of my head first. Now since I have had a lot of time thinking about it I can finally say what the film does best and worst. Please be respectful, if I have made any mistakes I open to it and we can have a good discussion!

***We are strictly talking as an independent film first*** I know its based on the text written by Homer of course but let us see what lies on the surface first and what it is on its own. It tells the story of Odysseus, his journey back to his family but he is not the only one on a journey, like I have said before, this is the journey about the characters as well. Telemachus's journey about finding his dad, Penelope's journey of perseverence and his crewman's journey too. I feel like its highly engaging enough that it kept me glued to my seat, had my attention. 

***One aspect I found lacking*** was the first 2 acts of the film, it plays into it slow, the pacing just takes its time and during that time it felt weak, I felt unintrested in most parts of it but in last hour of the film is where it really shines. I dont think its a weak point because it has some payoff but at the same time it is because it needs to keep u entertained, after all cinema is for entertainment.

Another thing I heard about this film is being "***high school project***" of Nolan's films but after actually thoroughly reviewing it I didnt felt so at all, a lot of hard work has went into the film from being shot in 100% IMAX cameras (which was already considered to be impossible to do before" working around restrictions during shooting, creating true to life sets, music using authentic instruments to shooting on location the list goes on. I feel that its Nolan's most practical and authentic film yet ***but it automatically does not make it his best film of all time***

There is a lot to be said when now we compare it to ***The Odyssey written by Homer***, Some of the people have pointed out that it turned the concept of ***Zeus's law which the film is highly revolved around*** and made it a mess, Xenia as describes in the text is wayy fundamentally different which I agree but I found this one interesting [https://www.reddit.com/r/classics/s/DTBFkcVFBK](https://www.reddit.com/r/classics/s/DTBFkcVFBK)  
which explains better how ***Nolan's interpretation of the Odyssey*** does work well on. Starting from the fact that it draws parrallel to our lives and most importantly it conveys the journey of self discovery very well. ***After all the story is about the journey of our own, how we in our own lives long to get back to the things or moments we love*** which is the centeral theme of the movie, not just another interpretation of the homeric text.

Another negative I can find is that it uses ***too much modernization*** to people's liking like the obvious use of modern generation dialogue to the dress appearing out of place to the own time its set in and some interesting casting choices but its his interpretation of it, its a modern retelling for the audience, even though it got many things wrong ***we cannot deny the fact that it has sparked a huge influence on Greek history as a whole, to the point Im writing this*** after doing my own research. ***Even the message it tried to convey might have not been clear or perfect, BUT it set successfully set out to do one task that is to spark interest in Greek culture.***

Another ***negative*** I have seen is how Odysseus is portrayed in this film compared to the original, where he is actually a master strategist and pragmatic where in this film he is depicted as a warrior with a burden carrying guilt but in my perspective it works ***really well for HIS interpretation not the text***

One cannot deny the impact the film has made intertwining Greek culture with pop culture history like never before, nor can one deny the effort put into this film. ***While it will not remain the best adaptation or the best Nolan film BUT it will remain a great film of this year.***

***Thank you for reading!***

### Top 1 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The editing is a mess and I dont feel the cinematography captured the epic scale of the story or the fact they made such a big deal of filming it all in Imax. Like the preview of Dune at my Imax showing felt way grander than the Odyssey.
  - I completely understand why you feel that way. The reason it didn't feel that "Grand" or large scale enough like it should be is because he chose to keep it grounded and realistic where it works well in some parts but not in others. I feel like editing was fine though as the movie was easy enough to be followed through and like the text it bounced back and forth between Odysseus and people back in Ithaca.

## 3. The dune movies aren’t that politically insightful

**Score:** 0
**Body:** The charismatic leader that betrays the revolution is far from a new claim. In the spirit of the 60s with all the anticolonial Revolution this actually had a referent, but 99% of the American left (the fascists on the right of course will just cognitively dissociate witj these kinds of points so I don’t think they’re a relevant audience to consider) knows this point. So this isn’t breaking new ground nor really offering a new perspective on this tired issue. This doesnt mean there aren’t political questions that come from this— Obama and Mamdani have become messianic figures for their relative constituencies. The points about colonialism are well known. The west drains the world’s resources to get rich. As well as the bene gesserit, a secret cabal of elites running the world from behind the scenes.

For me, politically insightful movies raise problems that truly probe at really interesting concepts. The dark knight shows how the dangers in American’s fantasy for policing and law and order, how western desires for heroism contradict their desires for negative rights. There Will be Blood asks what is the foundation of this nation, what makes america America, what is the violence in the drive for greatness? It also makes insightful critiques of the beloved petty bourgeoisie, dispelling the innocent myths of small business owners. What makes them insightful is not that they’re “correct” or “incorrect,” but that they display things that really make you think.
